question.problem:
Using a trapezoidal sum with two equal subintervals, ${\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈${{field-1}}
.
question.worked_solution:
The general formula for the trapezoidal rule states that

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈\frac{1}{2}[q(a)+2(q({t}_{1})+q({t}_{2})+…+q({t}_{n-1}))+q(b)]Δt,
$$

where $n$ is the number of trapezoids and $Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}$ is the step size.

Here, we have the following values:

* The number of trapezoids is $n=2.$

* The corresponding interval is $[0,4],$ so we have $a=0$ and $b=4.$

* The step size is given by

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{4-0}{2}=2.
$$

Using the above values, the general formula becomes

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t≈\frac{1}{2}[q(0)+2q(2)+q(4)]\cdot 2.
$$

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the above expression gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}q(t)\,\text{d}t & ≈\frac{1}{2}[0+2(120)+108]\cdot 2 \\  & =240+108 \\  & =348.\end{aligned}
$$

shared_context.problem:
A campsite opens on the $1$st of May $(t=0)$ and closes after $8$ months. The number of customers in the campsite after $t$ months is modeled by a differentiable function $q$ for $0\le t\le 8.$ Some values for $q(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below.

| $t$ (months) | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $q(t)$ (customers) | $0$ | $59$ | $120$ | $92$ | $108$ | $85$ | $47$ | $18$ | $0$ |

earlier_parts.problem:
From the given data, the best forward difference approximation for the rate at which the number of customers was changing on June $1$st is

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
customers per month.

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that June $1$st corresponds to $t=1.$

We use the forward difference approximation formula

$$
{q}^{′}(t)≈\frac{q(t+h)-q(t)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible. In this case, we choose $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1+1)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(2)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{120-59}{1} \\  & =61.\end{aligned}
$$

So, using a forward difference approximation, the rate of change in the number of customers on June $1$st is approximately $61$ customers per month.

earlier_parts.problem:
From the given data, the best backward difference approximation for the rate at which the number of customers was changing on June $1$st is

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
customers per month.

feedback.worked_solution:
Again, we use the fact that June $1$st corresponds to $t=1.$

We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{q}^{′}(t)≈\frac{q(t)-q(t-h)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible. In this case, we choose $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1)-q(1-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(1)-q(0)}{1} \\  & =\frac{59-0}{1} \\  & =59.\end{aligned}
$$

So, using a backward difference approximation, the rate of change in the number of customers on June $1$st is approximately $59$ customers per month.
